title: Put the Destination in the Frame
author: John Seel
summary: In this guest post on Aaron Renn's site, Dr. John Seel argues that public talk about men is framed around problems such as the crisis of boys and men, rather than the destination we want men to reach. A frame tells us how to interpret facts, and people keep the frame while rejecting facts that do not fit it. Using fatherlessness as the example, he shows that asking what kind of community forms committed husbands and fathers pulls in coaches, teachers, churches, older men and culture, and moves attention upstream to a boy's formation at ages three, eight or twelve. He warns that problems have gravity: money, nonprofits and careers orbit them until a system manages a problem without preventing it. His rule is that programs address problems while ecologies cultivate conditions, so the desired good must be in the frame from the start.
points: Seel argues that frames determine how facts are interpreted, so a problem-centered frame keeps the problem as the organizing category of reform.
Reframing fatherlessness as the question of which community forms committed husbands and fathers makes it a task for families, schools, churches, coaches and friends, not only social workers.
Because formation happens at ages three, eight or twelve, the goal should be forming a healthy man rather than reforming an unhealthy one.
He notes that problems have gravity, so institutions can become expert at managing a problem while having a vested interest in its continuing.
Boys need models, ambitions, responsibilities and people who expect something from them, in a picture of masculinity marked by courage, sacrifice, service, love and generativity.
quotes: If you frame an issue by its problem, the problem will remain part of the issue. If you want to solve a problem, the solution needs to become part of the original frame.
It’s as much or more about forming a healthy man rather than reforming an unhealthy one.
Before long, an entire system can become very good at managing a social problem without becoming equally good at preventing it.
We have to make an important distinction: Programs address problems. Ecologies cultivate conditions. We need both.
A problem frame asks: What are we trying to get away from? A generative frame asks: What are we trying to create?

If we constantly describe men in the language of failure, toxicity, immaturity, dysfunction, and deficiency, we should not be surprised when young men have trouble imagining a compelling version of adulthood.
The question is not simply how we keep boys from becoming bad men. It is what kind of men we are calling them to become.
